books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the idea of Manifest Destiny motivated American territorial expansion in the period 1844–1860.

documents.title: O'Sullivan names Manifest Destiny
documents.source: John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July 1845. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: O'Sullivan, a Democratic editor, writing in a party magazine to defend the annexation of Texas. He coined the phrase “manifest destiny” in this editorial.
documents.text: And that claim is by the right of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions. California will, probably, next fall away from the loose adhesion which, in such a country as Mexico, holds a remote province in a slight equivocal kind of dependence on the metropolis.

documents.title: Polk's inaugural on Texas and Oregon
documents.source: James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Polk, the newly inaugurated Democratic president, stating his expansionist program in his first address to the nation.
documents.text: To enlarge its limits is to extend the dominions of peace over additional territories and increasing millions... Our title to the country of the Oregon is “clear and unquestionable,” and already are our people preparing to perfect that title by occupying it with their wives and children.

documents.title: Map of the United States, including Oregon, Texas, and the Californias
documents.source: John Haven, map published by Haven & Emmerson, New York, 1846. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A commercial broadside map printed in New York at the outset of the Mexican War, picturing Texas, Oregon, and the Californias inside an American frame, with the boundary the United States claimed.

documents.title: Thoreau refuses the government
documents.source: Henry David Thoreau, “Resistance to Civil Government,” published May 1849 in Aesthetic Papers. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Thoreau, a Massachusetts writer, published this essay in 1849 after refusing to pay a tax in protest against slavery and the Mexican War.
documents.text: How does it become a man to behave toward the American government to-day? I answer, that he cannot without disgrace be associated with it. I cannot for an instant recognize that political organization as my government which is the slave's government also.

documents.title: Polk confirms the gold in California
documents.source: James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Polk reporting to Congress on the gold discovery in California, using official reports to confirm stories that seemed unbelievable.
documents.text: The accounts of the abundance of gold in that territory are of such an extraordinary character as would scarcely command belief were they not corroborated by the authentic reports of officers in the public service, who have visited the mineral district, and derived the facts which they detail from personal observation.

documents.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Article IX
documents.source: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed February 2, 1848 (ratified text). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The peace treaty ending the Mexican War, setting the terms on which Mexicans in the ceded lands would become Americans.
documents.text: The Mexicans who, in the territories aforesaid, shall not preserve the character of citizens of the Mexican Republic... shall be incorporated into the Union of the United States, and be admitted at the proper time (to be judged of by the Congress of the United States) to the enjoyment of all the rights of citizens of the United States...

documents.title: Donation Land Claim Act, Section 4
documents.source: Donation Land Claim Act, September 27, 1850, Section 4. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress granting free land in Oregon Territory to white settlers, passed in September 1850.
documents.text: There shall be, and hereby is, granted to every white settler or occupant of the public lands, American half-breed Indians included, above the age of eighteen years, being a citizen of the United States... the quantity of one-half section, or 320 acres of land, if a single man, and if a married man the quantity of one section, or 640 acres; one-half to himself and the other half to his wife, to be held in her own right.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which Manifest Destiny motivated American territorial expansion in 1844–1860, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of motivation does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the westward migration of the 1840s, the Texas Revolution, or the Oregon boundary dispute.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the role of Manifest Destiny.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Wilmot Proviso of 1846, the Gadsden Purchase of 1853, or Perry's mission to Japan.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of motivation, explaining why expansion had other causes, or showing how the idea was contested.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Manifest Destiny was the language of American expansion in 1844–1860, but it was a justification more than a cause — it gave a moral frame to gains driven by land hunger, gold, and politics.
Context: By 1844 Texas was an independent republic, Oregon was disputed with Britain, and migrants were already crossing the continent on the overland trails.
Evidence: Documents 1–3 show the idea at work — O'Sullivan coining the phrase, Polk claiming Texas and Oregon, and a commercial map picturing a continent-wide nation. Documents 4–7 show its limits — Thoreau refusing the government, gold drawing migrants for profit rather than principle, a treaty absorbing Mexicans, and Congress giving away Oregon land to settlers.
Beyond the documents: The Wilmot Proviso of 1846 shows the idea splitting the nation over slavery, and the Gadsden Purchase of 1853 shows expansion continuing as a railroad bargain.
Sourcing: O'Sullivan wrote as a Democratic editor defending his party's policy; Thoreau wrote as a dissenter who had gone to jail over the war; the map was a commercial broadside meant to sell.
Complexity: The idea mattered most as language — it let Americans call conquest destiny, while the land itself was taken by treaty, war, purchase, and settlement.
